screens.title: Setting Up Your Unreal Engine 5 C++ Development Environment
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn how to prepare a solid development environment for Unreal Engine 5 using C++. We’ll walk through installing the Epic Games Launcher and the engine, choosing and configuring an IDE, creating a C++ project named MyFirstCPPProject, and verifying that your project compiles. A correctly configured environment matters because C++ grants access to engine internals and performance-sensitive systems that Blueprints cannot match. As an example, the Visual Studio workloads known as "Game development with C++" and "Desktop development with C++" provide the compilers and SDKs that Unreal needs to build projects; missing them is a common setup error that causes compilation to fail. You will also learn how the Unreal Editor’s Compile button and hot reloading speed iteration, and when a full editor restart is required. By the end you’ll be able to create a project, open the solution in your IDE, and compile safely. As you start, notice that setup prevents many future headaches — keeping tools correct is the first step to productive C++ development.

First, you will be able to install and configure Unreal Engine 5 and the supporting C++ development tools so that the editor and compiler work together. For example, installing Visual Studio with the correct workloads prevents missing SDK errors. Second, you will understand why the Visual Studio workloads exist and which components they provide, like the MSVC compiler and Windows SDKs, so you can troubleshoot missing toolchains. Third, you will create a new C++ project, open the generated solution in your IDE, and explore the editor’s key panels to find where content and C++ classes live. Finally, you will compile a project and use hot reloading to iterate quickly, while recognizing when a full editor restart is required. Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Competency Checks

Verify your setup with quick checks

Each milestone is a short verification you can perform after installation to ensure the next steps will succeed.

01 • Engine installed

Open the Epic Games Launcher and confirm your chosen engine version is listed in Library. If not, re-run the installer.

02 • Workloads present

In the Visual Studio installer, confirm "Game development with C++" and "Desktop development with C++" are selected and MSVC/Windows SDK components are installed.

03 • Project files generated

Create MyFirstCPPProject and check that a .uproject and a solution file exist in the project folder.

04 • Successful compile

Use the editor's Compile button, then inspect the Output Log or Visual Studio Error List to confirm a clean build.

Quick tip

If compilation fails, stop and inspect the installer selections first. Many errors stem from missing workloads rather than code bugs at this stage.

screens.title: Why choose C++ for Unreal Engine 5
screens.narratorSegment: C++ is the language that gives you the deepest control over Unreal Engine internals. Unlike Blueprint visual scripting, C++ lets you implement performance-sensitive systems, customize engine-level behavior, and access APIs that Blueprints can’t express or that would run too slowly in tight loops. A concrete example: when implementing a complex physics subsystem or an optimized AI pathfinder, C++ allows precise memory and threading control so you can reach the performance targets a shipped game needs. A common misconception is that Blueprints are always easier and just as capable; while Blueprints are excellent for prototyping and game logic, they do not replace C++ when you need raw performance, custom engine modules, or low-level memory handling. For beginners, a practical approach is to prototype gameplay in Blueprints and progressively move performance-critical code into C++ classes. This hybrid workflow keeps iteration fast while allowing you to extract and optimize hotspots. Key takeaway: learn to use both tools, but rely on C++ when performance and engine-level access are required. Which gameplay systems in your current project would benefit from native C++ performance? Why choose C++ for Unreal Engine 5 means use c++ for performance, engine access, and complex systems; use blueprints for rapid prototyping and high-level logic.. In practical terms, when and why raw c++ matters versus blueprints. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use C++ for performance, engine access, and complex systems; use Blueprints for rapid prototyping and high-level logic.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › C++ Rationale
Definition

C++’s role in UE5

C++ provides low-level control, direct engine API access, and performance benefits that Blueprints cannot match.

Concrete example
An optimized physics update loop for many moving actors is typically written in C++ to avoid Blueprint overhead.
Common misconception
Blueprints are not a full replacement for C++. They are complementary tools; use each where it fits best.
Key takeaway
Start with Blueprints for quick tests, then move performance-critical or engine-level features into C++.
Analogy

Blueprints are a sketch; C++ is the toolkit

Sketching with Blueprints helps you validate ideas quickly. When a sketch becomes production, you refine it with C++ tools for strength and performance.

When to choose C++
  • Physics and rendering paths
  • Custom engine modules
  • Performance hotspots
When Blueprints are fine
  • UI flow and event wiring
  • Rapid prototyping
  • Simple gameplay rules
Reflect

Identify one system in your current project that should start in Blueprints and later move to C++ for optimization.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Install UE5
Step-by-step

Install via Epic Games Launcher

1. Download Launcher
Install the Epic Games Launcher, then open it and sign into your account.
2. Library → Add Engine
Open the Unreal Engine tab and add a new engine version; pick the stable UE5 build you want to use.
3. Verify install
After download, confirm the engine entry appears in Library and can be launched.
Checks & tips
Select stable builds
Avoid preview releases for production work. If collaborating, standardize on an engine version.
Installation path
Choose a common path and ensure you have disk space; projects will reference this path.
Common mistake
Assuming the launcher icon equals the engine install. Verify in Library that the engine version is installed and launchable.
Test

Launch the engine and create a blank C++ project to confirm the editor opens and generates project files.

screens.title: Visual Studio on Windows — required workloads
screens.narratorSegment: On Windows, Visual Studio is the standard IDE for Unreal Engine C++ development. The critical step during installation is selecting the correct workloads. The two workloads you must include are "Game development with C++" and "Desktop development with C++." The game workload bundles components tailored to game engines, while the desktop workload supplies compilers and SDKs needed for native builds. Practically, these workloads install MSVC toolsets, Windows SDKs, and the build tools that Unreal uses to compile and link code. A likely mistake is installing Visual Studio without selecting workloads and assuming the IDE alone is sufficient. The result is typically compilation errors that mention missing compilers or undefined SDKs. For example, building a new project without MSVC will fail because no compiler is available to produce object files. If you ever see errors like "SDK not found" or linker failures right after creating a project, revisit the Visual Studio installer and add the workloads. This step prevents most early build failures and saves hours of debugging. Visual Studio on Windows — required workloads means install 'game development with c++' and 'desktop development with c++' to provide msvc, windows sdks, and build tools required by unreal.. In practical terms, which visual studio components unreal engine requires and why. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Visual Studio Workloads
Must-have workloads

Game & Desktop C++

These workloads install compilers, SDKs, and build tools Unreal requires to compile and link C++ projects.

Game development with C++
Includes toolchains and settings optimized for game projects and engine integration.
Desktop development with C++
Provides core MSVC compilers and Windows SDKs needed for native builds.
Checks & common mistakes
Verify MSVC and SDK
Open the Visual Studio installer summary and confirm MSVC v143 and Windows SDKs are selected.
Misconception
IntelliSense or editor features alone do not equate to a full compiler toolchain. A functioning editor without workloads often fails to build.
If build fails
Add workloads via the Visual Studio installer, then rebuild the project to clear missing-toolchain errors.
Tip

If collaborating, record the exact Visual Studio version and workloads used so teammates match the toolchain.

screens.title: Xcode on macOS — what you need
screens.narratorSegment: On Mac O S, Xcode is the primary IDE for Unreal C++ projects. While the chapter focuses mainly on Windows, the key point is that Xcode typically provides the necessary compilers and SDKs when installed from the App Store. Installing Xcode gives you Clang, the Mac O S SDKs, and the build environment that Unreal requires. A practical example: after installing Xcode, creating a C++ project will generate an Xcode workspace or project you can open to explore the generated source files and build configurations. A common misconception is that Mac users can skip an IDE and rely solely on the editor; without Xcode’s toolchain you will encounter compilation failures. Also note that Mac O S tooling behaves differently in details such as code signing and certain build paths, so double-check build errors in the Xcode build log when troubleshooting. If you see missing compiler errors on Mac O S, ensure Xcode and the command line tools are installed and up to date. The main benefit for Mac O S is that installing Xcode typically covers the necessary toolchain in one step.

screens.title: Create a new C++ project in UE5
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a new C++ project in Unreal Engine 5 is straightforward but requires a few deliberate choices. Open the engine and use the project browser. Under 'Games', choose a template. While a blank template gives you a clean slate, templates such as Third Person or First Person provide a playable character and level that are useful for testing your C++ changes quickly. Most importantly, set the project type to C++ rather than Blueprint. Name your project MyFirstCPPProject and choose a location that you will remember. For a minimal starting point, choose No Starter Content so the project is lighter and compiles faster; starter content can be added later if needed. After you click Create, Unreal will generate the. uproject file along with a Source folder and the IDE solution file. If generation fails, check available disk space and ensure the engine install is valid. As a concrete example, choosing the Third Person template speeds testing because you immediately have a character to preview physics and input code. The closing question: which template best supports your first experiments with C++? In practical terms, project template selection, naming, and starter content choices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Create Project
Step sequence

Create MyFirstCPPProject

  1. Open Unreal Engine and the Project Browser.
  2. Choose Games → select a template such as Blank or Third Person.
  3. Set Project Type to C++ and name the project MyFirstCPPProject.
  4. Choose No Starter Content for a lean setup.
  5. Click Create; wait for project files and the editor to open.
Practical note

Templates with a playable character help you test C++ gameplay code immediately after compile.

Generated files

MyFirstCPPProject/Source/MyFirstCPPProject/MyFirstCPPProject.cpp
MyFirstCPPProject/Source/MyFirstCPPProject/MyFirstCPPProject.h

Confirm

Open the generated solution file in your IDE to inspect the source tree and build settings.

screens.title: Unreal Editor panels you need to know
screens.narratorSegment: After creating a project, the Unreal Editor is where you interact with scenes and assets. Four panels are especially important for C++ workflow: the Viewport, World Outliner, Details Panel, and Content Browser. The Viewport is the interactive scene where you place and test actors; it’s where your gameplay changes become visible. The World Outliner lists all actors in the current level, which helps you locate the specific actor you want to modify from code. The Details Panel shows properties for a selected actor or asset; when you expose UPROPERTY members in your C++ class, they appear here for designers to tweak. The Content Browser organizes assets and C++ class Blueprints; when you create a new C++ class, compiled classes appear here as usable assets. A common mistake is assuming that changing a design property in the editor always updates serialized defaults in code — some changes only live in the level unless saved back. As a practical check, after compiling a new class, find it in the Content Browser and add it into the scene to see that it behaves as expected. Which panel will you use first when testing your new C++ actor?

screens.narratorSegment: When Unreal generates a C++ project it creates a solution file for your IDE. On Windows you’ll open the. sln in Visual Studio; on Mac O S you open the Xcode project. Typical files include the top-level. uproject, a Source folder, and modules such as MyFirstCPPProject. h and MyFirstCPPProject. cpp. Opening these files shows you the basic game module class and the module startup code that registers the module with the engine. A concrete example: the module’s primary. cpp contains startup and shutdown hooks where you can register engine systems. A common misconception is that the IDE file view is read-only; you will edit these files, add classes, and build from the IDE. After a successful build, you can switch back to the editor and use hot reload to push simple changes into the running editor.

screens.title: Compile from Unreal Editor and Hot Reload
screens.narratorSegment: Unreal Engine supports compiling C++ both from your IDE and directly from the editor using the Compile button. Using the editor’s Compile is convenient for small changes because it triggers the engine’s hot reload mechanism. Hot reload attempts to recompile changed modules and inject the new code into the running editor instance without a full restart, which speeds up iteration. A concrete scenario: change a simple function body in an actor class, click Compile in the editor, and test the updated behavior immediately in the Viewport. However, hot reload is not perfect. When you make fundamental changes such as adding or removing UPROPERTY or UFUNCTION declarations, changing class hierarchies, or modifying memory layouts, the editor may not reload correctly and you should perform a full editor restart to ensure stability. A common misconception is to expect hot reload to handle every change; instead treat it as an iteration aid for small edits and rely on restarts for structural changes. When compilation fails, inspect the Output Log in the editor or the Error List in Visual Studio to find the precise compiler or linker messages. The closing takeaway: use hot reload for rapid edits, and don’t hesitate to restart when changes are structural.

screens.title: Common compilation and setup issues
screens.narratorSegment: Many early development roadblocks come from setup issues rather than bugs in your gameplay code. The most common symptom is a build failure immediately after creating a project. If you see errors complaining about missing compilers, SDKs, or undefined toolchains, the likely cause is an incomplete Visual Studio installation or missing Xcode command line tools on Mac O S. Another frequent issue is linker errors arising from incorrect include paths or conflicting third-party plugins. When you encounter a failure, your first actions should be to open the Output Log in the editor and the Error List in Visual Studio to capture the exact messages. These messages usually indicate a missing workload, a path problem, or a syntax error. For example, an "SDK not found" message typically points to missing Windows SDK components in the Visual Studio installer. A practical troubleshooting flow: verify workloads in the installer, rebuild the IDE solution, and then try the editor Compile. If plugin conflicts arise, temporarily disable third-party plugins and rebuild. The key misconception to avoid is assuming the code is wrong before checking the environment; often the setup is the root cause.

As an example, the Visual Studio workloads known as "Game development with C++" and "Desktop development with C++" provide the compilers and SDKs that Unreal needs to build projects; missing them is a common setup error that causes compilation to fail. You will also learn how the Unreal Editor’s Compile button and hot reloading speed iteration, and when a full editor restart is required. By the end you’ll be able to create a project, open the solution in your IDE, and compile safely. As you start, notice that setup prevents many future headaches — keeping tools correct is the first step to productive C++ development.

Second, you will understand why the Visual Studio workloads exist and which components they provide, like the MSVC compiler and Windows SDKs, so you can troubleshoot missing toolchains. Third, you will create a new C++ project, open the generated solution in your IDE, and explore the editor’s key panels to find where content and C++ classes live. C++ is the language that gives you the deepest control over Unreal Engine internals.
